title: Common or proper?
instructions: Sort each noun. A common noun names any person, place or thing. A proper noun names a particular one and starts with a capital letter.

title: Capital hunt
instructions: Five proper nouns forgot their capital letters. Tap each one, then type it correctly.
text: Every saturday, my cousin elena and I take the bus to Lincoln Park. In july we watched a parade for the Fourth of July, and a band from texas played. Next year i want to march in it.

errors.explanation: Days of the week are proper nouns, so they always start with a capital.
A person’s name is a proper noun.
Months are proper nouns. (The second July already has its capital.)
Names of places (states, cities, countries) are proper nouns.
“I” is always a capital letter when you mean yourself.

questions.prompt: Which word in this sentence is a noun? “The tired hikers rested quietly.”
questions.explanation: “Hikers” names people. “Tired” describes them, “rested” is the action and “quietly” says how.
questions.hint: Which word names a person, place, thing or idea?

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses capital letters correctly?

options.text: We visited the Museum in Boston.
We visited the Boston Science Museum.
We visited the boston science museum.

questions.explanation: “Boston Science Museum” is the name of one particular museum, so each main word is capitalized. “the museum” on its own is a common noun.

questions.prompt: Which word is a proper noun?
questions.explanation: Mars is the name of one particular planet. The others name any planet, rocket or astronaut.

title: Name it!
prompt: Write five sentences about a trip, real or imagined. Each sentence has its own task, listed above the writing box. Write them in order, one per line.
tips: Proper nouns name ONE particular person, place, day or thing: Maya, Lake Erie, Monday.
Common nouns name any one: a girl, the lake, a day.
Check every proper noun has a capital letter.

sentences.ask: Name the place you went, using a proper noun.
Say who went with you: a common noun and a name.
Say which day or month it was.
Describe something you saw there, using common nouns.
End with a sentence that names a street, building or park.

title: Touch it, feel it, group it
instructions: Sort the nouns. Concrete: you can see or touch it. Abstract: an idea or feeling. Collective: one word for a group.

title: Name the group
instructions: Pick the collective noun that fits each group.

items.sentence: A ___ of sheep wandered across the road.
items.hint: Birds come in this kind of group too.
items.explanation: Sheep and birds gather in a flock.

items.sentence: We heard a ___ of wolves howling.
items.explanation: Wolves hunt together in a pack.

items.sentence: A ___ of bees buzzed around the hive.
items.hint: Think of a busy, buzzing cloud.
items.explanation: Bees fly in a swarm.

items.sentence: The farmer led a ___ of cows to the barn.
items.explanation: Cows, elephants and deer move in a herd.

items.sentence: A ___ of fans waited outside the stadium.
items.explanation: A large group of people is a crowd.

items.sentence: The ___ sang three songs at the concert.
items.explanation: A group of singers is a choir.

title: Find the ideas
instructions: Tap the four abstract nouns: ideas or feelings you can’t see or touch.
text: Jamal felt a wave of fear as he stepped onto the stage. Then he remembered his grandmother’s advice: courage is just fear that keeps going. He played the first note, and his worry turned into joy.
explanation: Fear, courage, worry and joy are feelings: you can’t hold them, but you know them. Stage, grandmother and note are concrete nouns.

title: Big ideas, real things
prompt: Write five sentences about a time you or a character worked with a group. Follow each task in order, one sentence per line.
tips: Abstract nouns name ideas and feelings: hope, pride, friendship.
Collective nouns name a group as one thing: team, class, band, crowd.
Pair an abstract noun with something concrete so the reader can picture it: “Pride glowed on her face.”

sentences.ask: Name the group, using a collective noun (team, class, band…).
Describe the place with two concrete nouns.
Say how someone felt, using an abstract noun.
Show a problem the group had.
End with an abstract noun that sums up what you learned.

title: One, two, many
instructions: Type the plural of the word in brackets.

items.sentence: We packed the books into three ___ (box).
items.hint: Words ending in x, s, ch or sh add -es.
items.explanation: box → boxes: words ending in x add -es.

items.sentence: My aunt has lived in four different ___ (city).
items.hint: Consonant + y: change the y to i and add -es.
items.explanation: city → cities: a consonant before the y, so y becomes ies.

items.sentence: The ___ (child) ran to the playground.
items.hint: This one is irregular: it doesn’t add -s at all.
items.explanation: child → children is an irregular plural.

items.sentence: Orange ___ (leaf) covered the path.
items.hint: Many words ending in f change to -ves.
items.explanation: leaf → leaves: the f changes to v, then add -es.

items.sentence: Two ___ (mouse) hid behind the fridge.
items.hint: Irregular: the vowel changes, like foot → feet.
items.explanation: mouse → mice is an irregular plural.

items.sentence: The ___ (monkey) swung from branch to branch.
items.explanation: monkey → monkeys: a vowel (e) before the y, so just add -s.

items.sentence: The dentist checked all my ___ (tooth).
items.explanation: tooth → teeth is an irregular plural.

items.sentence: Ten ___ (sheep) grazed on the hill.
items.explanation: sheep stays sheep: one sheep, ten sheep.

questions.prompt: The bike belongs to one girl. Which is correct?
questions.explanation: One owner: add ’s → the girl’s bike.

questions.prompt: The locker room belongs to all the players. Which is correct?
questions.explanation: Plural owner ending in s: add just the apostrophe → the players’ locker room.

questions.prompt: The toys belong to the children. Which is correct?
questions.explanation: “Children” is already plural and doesn’t end in s, so add ’s → children’s.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?

options.text: The cookie’s are on the table.
The cookies are on the table.
The cookies’ are on the table.

questions.explanation: Nothing belongs to the cookies here, so the plural needs no apostrophe.

title: Apostrophe patrol
instructions: Five words have a plural or apostrophe mistake. Tap each one and type the fix.
text: The puppy's are asleep in a basket by the door. My brothers bed is covered in their toys, and the childrens shoes are in a pile. Mom says the two familys next door will take most of the puppies, and we will keep the smallest puppys blanket.

errors.explanation: More than one puppy, and nothing belongs to them: puppies, no apostrophe.
The bed belongs to my brother, so it needs an apostrophe: brother’s bed (or brothers’ if they share it).
The shoes belong to the children: children’s.
Consonant + y: change y to ies → families.
The blanket belongs to one puppy (the smallest), so add ’s: puppy’s blanket.

title: Mine, yours, the team’s
prompt: Write five sentences about a busy day at school or at home. Follow each task in order, one sentence per line.
tips: Plural: more than one (dogs, boxes, children).
One owner: add ’s (the dog’s bowl). More than one owner ending in s: add ’ (the dogs’ bowls).
An apostrophe never makes a plural: “three apples”, not “three apple’s”.

sentences.ask: Use a regular plural (add -s or -es).
Use an irregular plural: children, people, feet, mice, teeth…
Show something that belongs to one person (’s).
Show something that belongs to a group ending in s (s’).
Use a plural AND a possessive in the same sentence.

title: Pronoun jobs
instructions: Sort the pronouns by their job. Subject: does the action. Object: receives the action. Possessive: shows who owns something.

title: Pick the pronoun
instructions: Choose the pronoun that fits. Tip: cover up the other person and read the sentence again.

items.sentence: Sam and ___ built a robot for the science fair.
items.hint: Cover “Sam and”: would you say “me built a robot”?
items.explanation: “I built a robot” sounds right, so it’s “Sam and I”.

items.sentence: Grandpa went fishing with Leo and ___.
items.explanation: After “with” you need an object pronoun: “with me”, so “with Leo and me”.

items.sentence: ___ scored the winning goal.
items.explanation: The person doing the action needs a subject pronoun: she.

items.sentence: The coach gave ___ new jerseys.
items.explanation: They receive the jerseys, so it’s the object pronoun: them.

items.sentence: That tent is ours, and the blue one is ___.
items.hint: Which one can stand on its own without a noun after it?
items.explanation: “Theirs” stands alone. “Their” needs a noun after it: their tent.

items.sentence: My sister and ___ share a room.
items.explanation: “I share a room” → “My sister and I share a room.”

items.sentence: Ms Ortiz asked ___ students to line up.
items.explanation: “Asked us to line up”, so “asked us students”.

items.sentence: The cat licked ___ paw.
items.explanation: “Its” shows belonging. “It’s” means “it is”.

title: Swap in a pronoun
instructions: Repeating a noun sounds clunky. Rewrite each sentence, replacing the repeated noun with the right pronoun.

items.task: Replace the second “Maya’s” with a pronoun.
items.explanation: “Her” is the possessive pronoun for Maya.

items.task: Replace “the twins” at the end with a pronoun.
items.source: We invited the twins because we like the twins.
answers: We invited the twins because we like them.
hints: Use the object pronoun for more than one person.
items.explanation: The twins receive the action, so the object pronoun is “them”.

items.task: Replace the second “Dad” with a pronoun.
items.source: Dad said Dad would drive us.
answers: Dad said he would drive us.
items.explanation: Dad is doing the driving, so the subject pronoun is “he”.

items.task: Replace “the book” at the end with a pronoun.
items.source: I found the book and returned the book to the library.
answers: I found the book and returned it to the library.
I found the book and returned it to the library
items.explanation: “It” replaces one thing.

title: Pronouns at work
prompt: Write six sentences about a game, match or competition. Follow each task in order, one sentence per line.
tips: Subject pronouns do the action: I, he, she, we, they.
Object pronouns receive it, and come after words like with, to, for: me, him, her, us, them.
Test a pair by covering the other person: “Sam and I won” → “I won”.

sentences.ask: Start with a subject pronoun doing an action.
Use an object pronoun after a verb (told him, helped us).
Use a pair as the subject: “My friend and I…”
Use a pair after with, for or to: “with Ana and me”.
Use a possessive pronoun before a noun (my, our, their).
Use a possessive pronoun on its own (mine, ours, theirs).

questions.prompt: The dogs wagged ___ tails.
questions.explanation: “Dogs” is plural, so the pronoun is plural too: their.

questions.prompt: The team celebrated ___ first win.
questions.explanation: A collective noun acting as one group takes a singular pronoun: its.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is clear?

options.text: When Ana met Priya, she smiled.
When Ana met Priya, Priya smiled.
When she met her, she smiled.

questions.explanation: With two people in the sentence, “she” could mean either. Using the name makes it clear.

questions.prompt: Every student needs ___ own pencil.
questions.explanation: “Their” is the possessive and works for one person whose gender we don’t know. (“His or her” is also correct.)

title: Who do you mean?
instructions: Each sentence has a pronoun that could mean two people. Rewrite it so it’s clear, using the name.

items.task: Make it clear that Leila won.
items.source: Maya told Leila that she had won the prize.
answers: Maya told Leila that Leila had won the prize.
hints: Which word could mean Maya or Leila?
Replace “she” with the name of the winner.
items.explanation: Swapping “she” for “Leila” removes the doubt.

items.task: Make it clear that the bike was Omar’s.
items.source: Omar and Ben fixed his bike.
answers: Omar and Ben fixed Omar's bike.
Omar and Ben fixed Omar’s bike.
hints: Use the possessive form of the name: Omar’s.
items.explanation: “Omar’s bike” says exactly whose bike it was.

items.task: Make it clear that Mom’s phone rang.
items.source: Mom called Aunt Rosa while her phone was ringing.
answers: Mom called Aunt Rosa while Mom's phone was ringing.
Mom called Aunt Rosa while Mom’s phone was ringing.
items.explanation: Naming the owner makes it clear.

title: Pronoun detectives
instructions: Five pronouns are wrong. Tap each one and type the right pronoun.
text: Me and Jada joined the robotics club last fall. The members built a robot, and they gave it a name. Our coach helped Jada and I with the wires. The wheels kept losing its grip, so us tried rubber bands. Now the trophy is our’s!

errors.explanation: “Me” is doing the action (joined), so it needs the subject pronoun. Better still: “Jada and I joined…”.
After “helped”, the pronoun receives the action: “helped Jada and me”.
“Wheels” is plural, so the pronoun is too: their grip.
“Us” is doing the trying, so it needs the subject pronoun: we tried.
Possessive pronouns never have an apostrophe: ours, yours, theirs.

title: Two friends, one problem
prompt: Write a paragraph (6–10 sentences) about two friends solving a problem together. Use pronouns so you don’t repeat names, but use a name whenever “he”, “she” or “they” could mean either friend.
tips: Introduce both friends by name first.
After a sentence with both names, start the next with a name, not “he” or “she”.
Check that every pronoun agrees: one person → he/she/they, more than one → they; things → it/they.

title: Nouns & Pronouns check
instructions: Ten questions on everything in this unit. You need 8 or more right (80%) to pass. If you don’t pass, you’ll see what to review and get new questions to try again.

questions.prompt: Which word is a proper noun?
questions.explanation: The Pacific is one particular ocean, so it’s a proper noun with a capital.

questions.prompt: Which sentence needs a capital letter that it doesn’t have?
questions.explanation: Months are proper nouns: October.

questions.prompt: In “The scientist studied the volcano near Naples,” which nouns are common?
questions.explanation: “Scientist” and “volcano” name any scientist or volcano; Naples is a particular city.

questions.prompt: Which word is an abstract noun?
questions.explanation: Honesty is an idea; you can’t see or touch it.

questions.prompt: Which word is a collective noun?
questions.explanation: An orchestra is one word for a group of musicians.

questions.prompt: “Her kindness surprised everyone.” What kind of noun is “kindness”?
questions.explanation: Kindness is a quality, an idea, so it’s abstract.

questions.prompt: A group of fish swimming together is called a…
questions.explanation: Fish swim in a school (or a shoal).

questions.prompt: What is the plural of “bench”?
questions.explanation: Words ending in ch add -es: benches.

questions.prompt: What is the plural of “story”?
questions.explanation: Consonant + y: change y to i and add -es → stories.

questions.prompt: Which plural is correct?
questions.explanation: foot → feet is an irregular plural.

questions.prompt: What is the plural of “knife”?
questions.explanation: Many words ending in -fe change to -ves: knives.

questions.prompt: The tail belongs to one cat. Which is correct?
questions.explanation: One owner: add ’s.

questions.prompt: The coats belong to several girls. Which is correct?
questions.explanation: Plural owner ending in s: add just the apostrophe.

questions.prompt: Which is correct?
questions.explanation: “Men” is plural without an s, so add ’s: men’s.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses an apostrophe correctly?
questions.explanation: Only (b) shows belonging: the peel of the banana. Plurals don’t take apostrophes.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
questions.explanation: The people doing the action need the subject pronoun “I”, and it’s polite to put yourself last.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.

options.text: The prize was shared between you and I.
The prize was shared between you and me.
The prize was shared between yourself and I.

questions.explanation: After a preposition like “between”, use object pronouns: you and me.

questions.prompt: “Coach thanked ___ for helping.” Which pronoun fits?
questions.explanation: They receive the thanks, so use the object pronoun: them.

questions.prompt: Which word is a possessive pronoun that can stand on its own?
questions.explanation: “Yours” stands alone: “The red one is yours.” “Your” needs a noun after it.

questions.prompt: Which is correct?
questions.explanation: “Its” shows belonging; “it’s” means “it is”; “its’” is never correct.

questions.prompt: The students put ___ bags on the shelf.
questions.explanation: “Students” is plural, so the pronoun is plural: their.

questions.prompt: The tree dropped ___ leaves.
questions.explanation: One tree, so the singular possessive: its.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is clearest?

options.text: Dad told Grandpa that he needed glasses.
He told him that he needed them.

questions.explanation: In (a), “he” could be Dad or Grandpa. In (b), it’s clear Grandpa needs glasses.

questions.prompt: “Lucia and Mei raced to the finish, and she won.” What’s the problem?
questions.explanation: With two girls named, “she” is unclear. Use the winner’s name.

title: Unit check: a scene to remember
prompt: Write a paragraph (at least 6 sentences) about a celebration, game or trip with a group of people. Show off this unit: use proper nouns with capitals, a collective noun, an abstract noun, plurals and possessives, and pronouns that are the right kind and clear.
tips: Checklist: 2+ proper nouns · a collective noun (team, class, crowd) · an abstract noun (joy, pride) · a possessive (Maya’s, the players’).
Use “I” and “me” correctly: “my friends and I”, “with my friends and me”.
Read it aloud. Is every “he”, “she” and “they” clear?
